# Does Seeing Your Breath Pacing Work Better Than Just Hearing It?

**A single-person EEG test comparing sound-only vs. visual-and-sound cues for coherent breathing**

## Introduction

Coherent breathing consists of inhaling for six seconds, and exhaling for six seconds, averaging 5 breath cycles a minute or 0.1 Hz. That rate sits on the resonance frequency of the human cardiovascular system, which is why it turns up everywhere from heart rate variability (HRV) biofeedback to clinical anxiety protocols. 

The protocol and instructions for this breathing exercise are well defined in casual guides and scientific literature; however, **the best way to signal when to inhale and exhale is still unclear.**

Currently, almost every breathing app makes a design choice here based on aesthetic grounds rather than measured ones. Some apps will use a tone that swells and fades, a circle that expands and contracts, or a voice counting you down (Fig. 1). Given the numerous alternatives, I sought to understand if the guidance format changes how easily a person holds the rhythm and therefore changes the intervention itself.

![][image1]  
**Figure 1\.** *Common sensory pacing guidance modalities utilized in digital coherent breathing interventions.*

My prediction going in came from an earlier pilot with a [Muse 2 headband](https://choosemuse.com/products/muse-2) and its stock app. Doing coherent breathing with my eyes open, I saw visibly greater HRV modulation than with my eyes closed; with my eyes closed I noticed far more mind-wandering and had a harder time holding focus. 

Meanwhile the Muse's alpha-based "calm" score barely moved from baseline at all, which I thought was due to the device's very limited sensor count (4 channels). From that I formed the hypothesis that **a visual pacing channel should outperform audio alone.** 

That’s why I moved to a [14-channel Emotiv Epoc X](https://www.emotiv.com/epoc-x) for this study. The added coverage gave me the resolution needed to track the spatial brain activity, allowing me to finally test whether what I see actually outperforms what I hear.

To do this, I designed a multi-session experiment comparing a resting baseline against two distinct 5-minute breathing conditions. The first one was guided by synchronized audio and visual cues, while the second one was driven entirely by audio. 

By tracking real-time cognitive metrics (e.g., stress, attention, and engagement) across these phases, my main aim was to definitively measure if adding a visual anchor changes the mental efficacy of the breathwork.

## Method

I ran three full sessions on myself with an Emotiv Epoc X (14 channels, saline sensors), using [Emotiv Studio](https://www.emotiv.com/studio) to configure the experiment and compute its built-in Performance Metrics: 

* Stress  
* Attention  
* Engagement  
* Excitement  
* Interest 

Each session contained both conditions: 

1. 240-second seated resting baseline  
2. 5-minute audio & video guided block  
3. 5-minute audio-only block

![][image2]  
**Figure 2\.** *Experimental timeline showing baseline rest, audio & video guided breathing, and audio-only guided breathing blocks repeated across three sessions (N=1).*

Moreover, breathing was 6 s in / 6 s out, seated upright. My eyes were open for every phase of every session, including baseline and both guided blocks. 

The audio pacing cue was built in Logic Pro and the synchronized visual animation in TouchDesigner, both driving the same 6 s/6 s cycle. Emotiv Studio aggregated the three sessions into a final Insights Report, and the numbers below are that report's.

## Results

All Performance Metrics were computed directly by Emotiv Studio's machine learning algorithms. The values below are baseline-corrected, meaning each number represents the net change from that session’s 240-second resting baseline (Table 1).

| Performance Metric | Audio & Video | Audio-Only | Observation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Stress** | −26.99 | \+0.52 | A\&V drove a substantial reduction; audio showed a negligible increase. |
| **Excitement** | −19.39 | −5.58 | Both lowered arousal, but A\&V drove a much deeper state of calm. |
| **Engagement** | \+12.85 | \+4.78 | A\&V produced significantly higher immersion in the exercise. |
| **Attention** | \+2.25 | \+1.80 | Both modalities effectively sustained baseline focus. |
| **Interest** | −14.85 | −1.77 | Both fell, but A\&V experienced a much sharper drop. |

**Table 1\.** *Mean baseline-corrected changes in neurocognitive and affective performance metrics across audio & video (A\&V) and audio-only coherent breathing conditions (N=1).*

### Affective and Arousal Metrics

The two guidance modalities showed the sharpest divergence in markers of physiological and affective arousal. The audio & video condition produced a substantial reduction in “Stress” relative to baseline (−26.99), whereas the audio-only condition yielded a negligible increase (+0.52) (Fig. 3).

![][image3]

**Figure 3\.** *Mean baseline-corrected change in Stress across audio & video and audio-only coherent breathing conditions (N=1).*

Both modalities resulted in a decrease in Excitement, though the magnitude differed notably. The audio & video condition drove a deeper reduction in this metric (−19.39) compared to the audio-only condition (−5.58) (Fig. 4). 

![][image4]

**Figure 4\.** *Mean baseline-corrected change in Excitement across audio & video and audio-only coherent breathing conditions (N=1).*

Taken together, the combined visual and auditory pacing appeared to facilitate a much steeper drop in overall affective arousal.

### Cognitive Engagement and Attentional State

Measures of focus and task immersion yielded mixed directional changes. Both modalities successfully maintained baseline “Attention”, with slight positive increases observed in both the audio & video (+2.25) and Audio-only (+1.80) conditions (Fig. 5).

![][image5]

**Figure 5\.** *Mean baseline-corrected change in Attention across audio & video and audio-only coherent breathing conditions (N=1).*

However, task immersion (measured as “Engagement) rose more significantly during the audio & video block (+12.85) compared to the Audio-only block (+4.78) (Fig. 6). 

![][image6]

**Figure 6\.** *Mean baseline-corrected change in cognitive engagement across audio & video (A\&V) and audio-only coherent breathing conditions (N=1).*

Conversely, “Interest” decreased in both conditions, with the audio & video modality demonstrating a substantially sharper decline (−14.85) than Audio alone (−1.77) (Fig. 7).

![][image7]

**Figure 7\.** *Mean baseline-corrected change in Interest across audio & video (A\&V) and audio-only coherent breathing conditions (N=1).*

### Electrophysiological Findings

Beyond the computed performance metrics, three distinct patterns emerged from the raw electrophysiological recording:

1. **Global Band Power:** The audio-only condition exhibited higher relative power across all five measured frequency bands (theta, alpha, low beta, high beta, and gamma) compared to the audio & video condition. The largest magnitude difference was observed in the theta band, followed by alpha, with progressively smaller gaps extending through low beta, high beta, and gamma (Fig. 8).

![][image8]

**Figure 8\.** *Mean relative band power across audio & video (A\&V) and audio-only coherent breathing conditions (N=1).*

2. **Topographic Distribution:** Direct visual inspection of the scalp topographic maps was consistent with the band power data. The audio-only condition displayed visibly more widespread cortical activity than the audio & video condition (Fig. 9).

![][image9]![][image10]

**Figure 9\.** *Scalp topographic maps and Frontal Alpha Asymmetry (FAA) across audio & video (A\&V) and audio-only coherent breathing conditions (N=1).*

3. **Frontal Alpha Asymmetry (FAA):** The computed FAA index was 0.026 for the Audio & Video condition and 0.141 for the Audio-only condition (Fig. 10).

![][image11]  
**Figure 10\.** *Mean Frontal Alpha Asymmetry (FAA) across audio & video (A\&V) and audio-only coherent breathing conditions (N=1).*

## Discussion

The results from these experiments suggest that it isn't the simple "video wins" story I expected.

On the affective and attentional side, adding a visual pacing channel resulted in much lower Stress, higher Engagement, a bigger drop in Excitement, and the same Attention. Electrophysiologically, the audio-only condition showed greater overall brain activation, with higher power across all frequency bands (most notably theta and alpha) and broader topographic activity. 

Those two observations suggest that audio-only was the harder condition, requiring more cortical work for an experience that ended up more tense and less immersive.

My own notes point the same way. Following the breathing and using my lung capacity well was distinctly harder in the audio-only condition. That improved with practice, but even after practice the audiovisual version stayed easier to follow, and a later session reinforced the impression rather than washing it out. So the pacing advantage held up across repeats.

The one metric that cuts against Audio & Video is Interest, which dropped further there than in audio-only. That's worth taking seriously as a content problem rather than a modality problem: the visual asset was designed as a pacing aid, not as something to hold aesthetic interest for five minutes, and it may simply have become monotonous. Different visual themes, color palettes, or motion patterns are an obvious thing to vary next.

While I was running the sessions I formed an idea about *why* the visual cue helps, and I want to be careful about its status. My sense is that the advantage comes from **anticipating the phase transition**, with a visual cue you can see how much time is left before inhale becomes exhale, so you arrive at the switch prepared rather than reacting to it. 

That's a temporal-prediction account, and it is a **post-hoc observation**, not something this study was designed to test or did test. The a priori prediction was only that visual pacing would outperform audio; the mechanism is a hypothesis for a future experiment. 

The natural test is a third condition: audio-only, but with a rising-pitch cue in the last few seconds of each phase, so the audio channel carries the same countdown information the animation does. If that closes the gap, temporal prediction is doing the work.

One design limitation to be explicit about: condition order was fixed in every session (i.e., Audio & Video always first, Audio always second) so order effects and modality effects cannot be separated here, and any future run should counterbalance.

## Conclusion

For my own practice, the audiovisual version is the one I'd reach for when the goal is dropping tension and staying with the rhythm; audio-only is what I'd use when I can't watch a screen, and it still moved Engagement and Attention in the right direction. 

The finding I most want to chase is the pacing question rather than the modality question, whether the visual cue's benefit is really about being able to see the phase transition coming. The next build is a rising-tone audio cue in the final seconds of each inhale and exhale, run against both existing conditions with the order counterbalanced.
